operations.evidence: The current contract, canonical HEAD 9e505bc119690fa75fb8a9ad17b90d6f40dd0300, UNCLAIMED owner, sequence 35 checkpoint, pickup_requested queue and open H-to-F blocker were verified before writes.
A 15-minute lease was claimed only for official-source and line-by-line website evidence; runtime and business writes remained disabled.
Police.uk describes force boundaries as constant; they remain operational police geography and not ONS LSOA geometry.
Neighbourhood policing team boundaries may change monthly and require a pinned month for contextual use.
Published boundary downloads include checksums; a downloaded file must match its recorded checksum before use.
The force stop-search endpoint defaults to the latest month even when that force has no data; an empty response was not treated as zero activity.
The availability endpoint is required to select a meaningful force-month before interpreting stop-search responses.
Force stop-search locations remain approximate and the records measure police activity rather than crime incidence.
Priority records contain issue and action narratives with dates for a force-specific neighbourhood.
Operational priority narratives were excluded from numeric crime or parcel-safety scoring.
Neighbourhood events expose operational titles, descriptions, addresses and ISO start/end dates.
Scheduled engagement and prevention events were not treated as crime incidents or parcel risk evidence.
Neighbourhood team responses contain personnel names, ranks, biographies and contact metadata.
Team size, rank mix and missing biographies were excluded from candidate scoring.
ONS confirms postcode boundaries commonly fail to align with administrative or statistical boundaries and centroid allocation can place addresses in the other area.
Postcodes change continuously and can be reused in another place after two years, so edition and termination status must be pinned.
NSPL allocates postcodes to Output Areas and references higher geographies through Census-population best fit.
ONSPD uses point-in-polygon relationships and assigns boundary-straddling postcodes by the mean grid reference of included addresses.
ONS postcode products are released quarterly in February, May, August and November; the edition must be recorded.
Postcode allocation was retained as a lookup method and not substituted for exact property or parcel point geometry.
NSUL performs direct UPRN-to-OA point-in-polygon assignment followed by best-fit higher-geography referencing.
ONSUD directly assigns UPRN grid references to administrative, health and other geographies by point-in-polygon.
NSUL and ONSUD relationship types were kept separate and cannot be silently interchanged.
UPRN products are released every six weeks and depend on address products; no runtime execution was inferred.
The IoD25 research report was pinned as the interpretation source for change over time and higher-geography summaries.
New data, methodologies and geographies make IoD25 less directly comparable with prior Indices.
Rank or decile movement was not represented as absolute deprivation change or a cardinal safety probability.
Only corrected spatial resources, the republished LSOA-to-LAD lookup and v2 IoD25 workbooks remain acceptable for joins.
Output Area population-size, homogeneity, boundary and confidentiality design principles were retained as geography context rather than parcel similarity evidence.
PEEL covers all 43 territorial forces but questions and methodologies change by inspection cycle, preventing simple grade time-series comparisons.
Crime-recording assessment is periodic and sample-based, and BTP scope differences can alter aggregates; inspection findings were not used as parcel confidence.

All 12 candidates remain unjoined at confidence zero; source rows 123-136 and operation rows 395-426 were published without a second runner, task, candidate value, business row, database write, migration or deployment.
